data.title: When did the Slavs arrive in the territory of present-day Slovakia?
data.excerpt: Our Slavic ancestors were far from the first inhabitants of the territory of present-day Slovakia – the Celts, the Púchov culture and Germanic peoples came before them. Both archaeology and written sources place the arrival of the Sklaveni, the bearers of the Prague culture, between the 470s and the first half of the 6th century.
data.metaTitle: When did the Slavs arrive in Slovakia?
data.metaDescription: When and from where the Slavs reached the territory of present-day Slovakia: bearers of the Prague culture crossing the Carpathian passes from the 470s onwards.

children.text: Slovakia is at present inhabited, as its majority nation, by the Slovaks, who formed in the course of the Middle Ages and the modern period out of the Slavs living here. Our Slavic ancestors, however, were far from being the first inhabitants of the territory of present-day Slovakia. As early as the Stone Age various cultures succeeded one another here which have no connection with the Slavs whatsoever. Likewise in the Bronze Age we know of a number of archaeological cultures from the territory of present-day Slovakia (the Nitra, Únětice, Otomani and Maďarovce cultures (Maďarovce was the original name of the village of Santovka, …where the culture was first described professionally, and the name of the culture has nothing whatsoever to do with the Hungarians – author’s note), the Velatice, Lusatian and others), whose ethnicity is not known; there is, however, no evidence on the basis of which any of these cultures could be linked with the Slavs. Nor do we know the bearers of the Early Iron Age cultures who inhabited our homeland (e.g. the Kalenderberg culture or the Vekerzug culture).
A MAP OF THE MIGRATION PERIOD HERE

The first light on the ethnic picture of the territory of Slovakia was shed only by the Celts, whom we begin to record in the territory of present-day Slovakia somewhere in the 5th century BC, when they occupied some of the lowland regions of Slovakia. In the northern parts of Slovakia we suppose that the Celts later mixed with the original population of the dying Lusatian culture and created the distinctive Púchov culture here, which we record in Slovakia from roughly the 3rd century BC until the 2nd century AD, that is, across the centuries around the turn of the era. Naturally, in the case of the Celtic, or Púchov, population (identified here with the tribe of the Cotini) we still cannot speak of Slavs. After the turn of the era the Germanic tribes of the Quadi penetrated into the territory of present-day Slovakia and considerably decimated the Púchov culture (but later became a part of it). At the same time we record Roman military fortifications in southern Slovakia, and at least a part of southern Slovakia came under the influence of the Roman Empire.
 
 In the 2nd century AD new waves of Germanic peoples arrived from the Elbe region, which forced the Romans to vacate the territory of Slovakia in part. In the following centuries Germanic occupation persisted here, ending only in the 5th century. The advance of the war bands of the Huns from the east in the last quarter of the 4th century marked the beginning of the period known as the Migration Period, which fills the 5th and the first half of the 6th century. The Huns put pressure on the other tribes that were settled to the west of them. In the first place they pressed on the Germanic Goths, under whose pressure further Germanic tribes in turn had to move, and ultimately the Quadi too had to move out of the territory of Slovakia.

We see that we are already somewhere at the turn of the 5th and 6th centuries and that Germanic peoples are still spreading out across the territory of Slovakia, while of our Slavic ancestors there is as yet neither sight nor sound here. But this picture was soon to change. Did the Slavs already exist at that time? And where would we have found them then? The answer is to be sought north-east of the Carpathian Basin, somewhere around the rivers Dniester, Pripyat and Dnieper.

In this period we record three archaeological cultures in the territory of Ukraine which are already considered Slavic. These are the Prague culture (whose bearers we identify with the Slavic tribe of the Sklaveni), the Penkovka culture (identified with the Antes) and the Kolochin culture (the Venethi). We Slovaks are most interested (despite its provocative name) precisely in the Prague culture (named after a site which, paradoxically, it settled only later), which of the three mentioned extended furthest west, in the basins of the rivers Dniester and Pripyat, and was bounded on the west by the outer part of the Carpathian range. Somewhere at the turn of the 5th and 6th centuries the Prague culture (that is, the Sklaveni) began to expand from its original seats in two directions: partly southwards, but above all north-westwards, which is to say into the Carpathian Basin as well.

children.text: Let us now return one last time to “Germanic” Slovakia, just before the arrival of our Slavic ancestors. As the eminent Slovak archaeologist Gabriel Fusek states in his article (in Historická revue 12/2016, p. 15), in the 5th century the seats of the Germanic Suebi extended across the north-western part of the Carpathian Basin. At the turn of 469 and 470, however, a fundamental change occurred here after the Ostrogoths, settled in Pannonia, crossed the frozen Danube and then destroyed the kingdom of the Suebi. A substantial part of them then withdrew westwards to the Alamanni, and only remnants of the Suebi stayed in the territory of Slovakia. This situation was in all probability exploited by the Sklaveni, who apparently began from then on to penetrate through the Carpathian passes into the territory of Slovakia. For this they apparently used the Veretsky Pass, the Dukla Pass and the valleys of the rivers Dunajec and Poprad. The territory of Slovakia was probably taken by the Sklaveni both by the eastern and by the northern route (from Poland). In the first half of the 6th century we then have it attested beyond doubt in the territory of present-day Slovakia, both archaeologically and in written sources, that the Slavs were already living here. In south-western Slovakia we may suppose that they were neighbours of the Germanic Lombards, who withdrew from there only at Easter in the year 568. The occupation of Slovakia by the Sklaveni thus evidently took place somewhere between the 470s and the first half of the 6th century and was completed after the withdrawal of the Lombards from south-western Slovakia in the middle of the 6th century. The Slavic Prague culture is then recorded here until somewhere around the middle of the 7th century, when part of the territory of present-day Slovakia came into the sphere of power of the Avar Khaganate.

children.text: To sum it all up, until the 5th century no Slavs lived in the territory of present-day Slovakia. Their invasion took place somewhere after the beginning of the 470s. In the course of a relatively short time they settled down here and survived, despite many calamities (for example the invasions of the Avars in the 7th–8th centuries, of the Hungarians in the 10th century, of the Mongols in the 13th century, …in the 16th–17th centuries and Magyarisation once again at the end of the 19th century), down to the present day, when our greatest calamity is our own politicians.
